label: Blue Note
bridge_case: Taylor's first Blue Note album and the studio work that crystallised his 'unit' concept of mobile ensemble architecture. It grows out of his 1950s post-bop experiments and the 1962 Nefertiti live recordings, and it opens directly onto Conquistador! and later large-group constructs such as the Cecil Taylor Unit.
rationale: Recorded May 19, 1966 at Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ [S2,S3] (obs); Released October 1966 on Blue Note as BLP 4237/BST 84237 [S2,S4,S5] (obs); Septet with two basses, two alto saxophones, trumpet, piano/bells and drums [S2,S3,S4,S5] (obs); AllMusic lists Avant-Garde Jazz, Free Improvisation and Free Jazz among its styles [S1] (obs); Widely regarded as one of the most structurally advanced and demanding statements of 1960s free jazz [S1,S2] (inf)

personnel_record.studio: Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs, NJ

personnel.name: Ken McIntyre
personnel.notes: Also credited on oboe and bass clarinet (S3, S4); primary horn here is alto saxophone.

notes: JazzDisco lists the session takes in a different order from the LP track order and assigns instruments by take number (e.g., Eddie Gale on takes 1, 2 and 5). Because the public LP order and the take-level order are not one-to-one, track-level instrument coverage is conservatively marked incomplete.
The 1987 CD reissue adds an alternate take of 'Enter Evening' that was not on the original LP.

scope_check.boundary_note: It is within the 1940–1979 window, but free jazz is a newly opened, permeable genre gate; this demanding avant-garde record directly tests the rubric's continuity and discovery-value requirements.

ballot.case_for: Taylor's first Blue Note album is a defining studio statement of 1960s free jazz: its mobile, rigorously organized "unit" architecture demonstrates that freedom from conventional harmonic and rhythmic roles need not mean absence of form. The May 19, 1966 septet has exceptional session gravity—Jimmy Lyons, Andrew Cyrille, Henry Grimes, Alan Silva, Eddie Gale, and Ken McIntyre—and its two-bass, multi-horn design opens from Taylor's earlier post-bop experiments toward Conquistador! and the later Cecil Taylor Unit (S2–S5). Its documented status as an advanced, demanding avant-garde work, alongside its Blue Note setting, makes it a powerful bridge record for a canon that intends to trace where post-bop language led (S1–S2).
ballot.case_against: The discovery test is a serious obstacle: Taylor's dense piano attack and rapidly shifting ensemble logic offer little conventional melodic, harmonic, or swing-based orientation to a listener encountering jazz cold. This is directly relevant to John's stated effort to study rather than prematurely embrace free jazz, and the dossier itself labels the album demanding. The evidence securely establishes session facts and genre classification, but does not provide robust independent canon-list or musician-testimony evidence for the stronger claim of broad consensus; Conquistador! may also present closely related ideas in a comparatively more approachable form.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John make this a deliberate free-jazz scope ruling, prioritizing a focused listen before deciding whether its structural achievement outweighs its formidable entry barrier.
